clue.text: Trivial cut at bottom of party mask

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece placed at the bottom of another comes after it

parts.note: a do is a party or celebration

indicators.note: cut means the word loses its final letter, docked like a tail

parts.note: something trivial is minor

explanation.surface: A trifling mask is trimmed at the bottom for a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' docks the last letter of MINOR to give MINO, and 'at bottom of' puts it below DO in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A domino is a small half-mask worn at masquerades, often with a hooded cloak.

clue.text: Recessive ear in marine animals identified in marine birds

indicators.note: in places the turned ear inside the word for the sea creatures

parts.note: seals are sea-dwelling mammals

indicators.note: recessive is read as receding or going backwards, so the word for ear is turned round

parts.note: lug is informal British for an ear

explanation.surface: A biology note about a recessive ear trait in sea mammals being found in seabirds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recessive' sounds like genetics but turns LUG into GUL, which goes 'in' SEALS. 'identified in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Gulls are common coastal birds that feed at sea.

clue.text: Description of dell enthrals one gloomily

indicators.note: enthrals means holds captive, so one word holds the other inside it

parts.note: a dell is a dingle, so something like a dell could be called dingly
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone describes a dell so gloomily that it captivates them.
explanation.walkthrough: DINGLY, an adjective formed from dingle (a wooded hollow), holds I.
explanation.definitionFit: Dingily means in a dull, drab, shabby manner, much as a gloomy room looks.

clue.text: Language cut to accommodate British English

indicators.note: to accommodate means to make room for, so the letters go inside

parts.note: to hew is to cut with an axe

explanation.surface: A language is trimmed to make room for British English.
explanation.definitionFit: Hebrew is the Semitic tongue of ancient Israel and modern Israel.

clue.text: Till operator, after initial theft, even more pale

indicators.note: after the initial is stolen, the first letter of the word is taken away

parts.note: a cashier operates a till in a shop

explanation.surface: A shop assistant goes paler still after a theft from the till.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initial theft' means the initial letter is stolen: CASHIER loses its C.
explanation.definitionFit: Ashy means pale as ash, so its comparative describes something paler.

clue.text: Artillery projectile: subjects under investigation much sought-after

parts.note: a detective's cases are matters being investigated
something hot is in great demand

explanation.surface: Investigators find a cannon shell is suddenly in high demand.
explanation.definitionFit: Case shot is a canister of small balls fired from a cannon, a kind of ammunition.

clue.text: Knocked over bronze pile — it's worth over a million dollars

definitions.text: it's worth over a million dollars

indicators.note: a pile knocked over is scattered, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone topples a heap of bronze worth a fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked over' looks like a reversal but is the anagram signal for BRONZE PILE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nobel award carries prize money of over a million dollars.

clue.text: Ideal page a newspaper's attached to

parts.note: a rag is a disparaging name for a newspaper
on means fixed to or attached to

explanation.surface: A model page attached to a newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A paragon is a perfect example, a model of excellence.

clue.text: 28 7 winner has upset women

indicators.note: upset means overturned or disturbed, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A literary prizewinner has upset some women.
explanation.walkthrough: 28 and 7 are LITERATURE and NOBEL PRIZE: George Bernard Shaw won in 1925.
explanation.definitionFit: George Bernard Shaw, the Irish playwright, received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1925.

clue.text: 28 7 winner, one telling tales

explanation.surface: A literary prizewinner is a storyteller.
explanation.walkthrough: To sing is slang for informing on someone, so a singer tells tales.
explanation.definitionFit: Isaac Bashevis Singer won the literature prize in 1978; an informer who sings to the police tells tales on others.

clue.text: 28 7 winner somehow appearing in grid more

indicators.note: somehow says the letters appear in some unspecified new arrangement

explanation.surface: A prizewinning author turns up in a crossword grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Nadine Gordimer, the South African novelist, won the literature prize in 1991.

clue.text: 28 7 winner contributing substantially to Indian films?

indicators.note: the name supplies a substantial opening part of the longer word, so the rest of it is dropped

parts.note: Bollywood is the Mumbai-based Hindi film industry

explanation.surface: A prizewinning writer plays a big part in Indian cinema.
explanation.walkthrough: The author's name forms the start of BOLLYWOOD; the YWOOD that follows is discarded.
explanation.definitionFit: Heinrich Böll, the German novelist, won the literature prize in 1972.

clue.text: 28 7 winner deserving to chase young women

indicators.note: to chase is to follow behind, so this word comes after the other

parts.note: gals is informal for girls or young women
worthy means deserving

explanation.surface: A deserving author pursues young women.
explanation.definitionFit: John Galsworthy, author of The Forsyte Saga, won the literature prize in 1932.

clue.text: 28 7 winner more frequently away? Good

parts.note: someone away more often is at home less, so the phrase reads as less in

explanation.surface: Asking whether a prizewinner is abroad more often, and finding that good.
explanation.walkthrough: Being away more often means being in less, read as LESS IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Doris Lessing, the British novelist, won the literature prize in 2007.

clue.text: Copies I'd distributed from time to time

indicators.note: distributed means spread out, so the letters are dealt into a new order

explanation.surface: Copies are handed out now and then.
explanation.definitionFit: Episodic means occurring at irregular intervals, now and then.

clue.text: 28 7 winner — stick with it, returning after a little time

indicators.note: after places the turned piece behind the others

parts.note: a cane is a walking stick
T is the abbreviation for time

indicators.note: returning means the word it is read backwards

explanation.surface: A prizewinner is told to persevere and come back after a short while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stick with it' looks like advice to persevere; it is CANE plus IT. 'returning' turns IT into TI, which follows T.
explanation.definitionFit: Elias Canetti, the Bulgarian-born writer, won the literature prize in 1981.

clue.text: Article not belonging to woman, but something else

parts.note: a is the indefinite article
taken as written
her is the possessive for a woman

explanation.surface: A thing that does not belong to a woman is something different.
explanation.definitionFit: Another means a different one, a further thing besides.

clue.text: Theatrical music at centre, possibly

indicators.note: possibly says the letters could be arranged in another way

explanation.surface: Music at the centre of a theatre, perhaps.
explanation.definitionFit: An entr'acte is an interlude, especially music played between acts of a play.

clue.text: Fifth scheme turned up stone globes

parts.note: a plan is a scheme
E is the fifth letter of the alphabet

indicators.note: in a down entry turned up means read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: st is the abbreviation for stone, the British weight of 14 pounds

explanation.surface: A fifth scheme turns up some stone globes.
explanation.walkthrough: ST, short for stone, a British weight of 14 pounds, is 'turned up' to TS.
explanation.definitionFit: Planets are spherical worlds, celestial globes orbiting a star.

clue.text: 28 7 winner rolled with pain, in torment

indicators.note: in torment suggests writhing agony, so the letters twist into a new order

explanation.surface: A prizewinner writhes in pain and agony.
explanation.definitionFit: Luigi Pirandello, the Italian dramatist, won the literature prize in 1934.

clue.text: A fondness for money? Certainly

parts.note: greed is an excessive love of wealth

explanation.surface: Is a love of money a good thing? Certainly.
explanation.definitionFit: Agreed is said to signal assent, like of course.

clue.text: Work to provide drinking water lasted, unexpectedly

indicators.note: unexpectedly suggests things turning out differently, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Work to supply drinking water lasted longer than expected.
explanation.definitionFit: To desalt seawater is to remove its salt so it can be drunk.

clue.text: 28 7 winner back in Trade Union for foodstuff

indicators.note: in places the turned name inside the union abbreviation
back means the name is read backwards

parts.note: Dario Fo, the Italian playwright, won the literature prize in 1997

explanation.surface: A literary prizewinner returns to the union for some food.
explanation.walkthrough: Here the laureate is not the definition: FO, 'back', is OF, inside TU.
explanation.definitionFit: Tofu is bean curd, a soya-based food.

clue.text: Mocks refugees?

explanation.surface: Is it mocking people who have fled?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags an invented sense: those who flee.
explanation.definitionFit: To fleer is to sneer or laugh scornfully; refugees are people who flee, read as fleers.

clue.text: 287 winner, chap returning in clutches of fool

indicators.note: in the clutches of means held inside, so one word sits within the other

parts.note: a moron is a fool

indicators.note: returning means the word is read backwards

parts.note: sir is a polite way to address a man

explanation.surface: A prizewinning man comes back in the grip of a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: SIR 'returning' gives RIS, held inside MORON. 287 is the clue's run-together of 28 7.
explanation.definitionFit: Toni Morrison, the American novelist, won the literature prize in 1993.

clue.text: 28 7 winner — exclamation about one from Scotland

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word goes round the other

parts.note: hey is an exclamation
ane is Scots for one

explanation.surface: A cry greets a Scot who won a prize.
explanation.definitionFit: Seamus Heaney, the Irish poet, won the literature prize in 1995.

clue.text: 28 7 winner absorbed in wrong ideas

indicators.note: absorbed in means taken up inside, so the name sits within the words

explanation.surface: A prizewinner is caught up in mistaken ideas.
explanation.definitionFit: André Gide, the French author, won the literature prize in 1947.

clue.text: Some drink in America's character, ignoring foremost in writing

parts.note: liter is the American spelling of litre, a measure of drink

indicators.note: ignoring foremost means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: a person's nature is their character

explanation.surface: Some drink shapes America's character, beyond its first writers.
explanation.walkthrough: LITER is the US spelling; NATURE 'ignoring foremost' loses N to give ATURE.
explanation.definitionFit: Literature is written work, books and poems collectively.
